title: TB8-09512
frame:
Forum: Refugee Appeal Division (appeal tribunal).
Parties: the appellant and the Minister; names are redacted.
Decision under review (from the opening paragraphs): XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX (the "Appellant"), a citizen of Portugal, appeals a decision of the Refugee Protection Division (RPD) denying his claim for refugee protection.
How the layers nest here: The RAD member is the author (layer 1). The appellant and the Minister make submissions to the RAD (layer 2). The RPD decision under appeal is layer 3, and what the claimant or the Minister said to the RPD, as reported, is layer 4.

paragraphs.text: XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX (the "Appellant"), a citizen of Portugal, appeals a decision of the Refugee Protection Division (RPD) denying his claim for refugee protection. He has not submitted new evidence in support of this appeal. The Appellant is not requesting an oral hearing. The Appellant asks the Refugee Appeal Division (RAD) to overturn the decision of the RPD and to find that the Appellant is a Convention refugee or a person in need of protection. In the alternative, the Appellant requests that the matter be returned to the RPD for a new hearing under a differently constituted panel.

The Appellant alleges that he fled Portugal in 2012 over fear of harm coming to him by former employees who threatened the Appellant because the Appellant failed to pay the workers their wages earned.
The Appellant was arrested in Canada by CBSA in September of 2015 for overstaying his visa.

The Appellant was interviewed at that time by CBSA and told CBSA, among other things, that "He has no fear in returning to Portugal but does not want to go back since things are bad in Portugal and there is no work," and that "He really likes living in Canada and feels that there are more work opportunities."1

The Appellant was then interviewed by the Minister's Delegate on 19 November 2015 during which interview the Appellant told the Minister's Delegate that the Appellant stayed in Canada (beyond his visa allowance) because he could not afford to support his family in Portugal because there was no job back home. In the same interview, the Appellant told the Minister's Delegate that he feared that people he owed money to wanted to kill him. In this same interview, the Appellant told the Delegate that on XXXX XXXX, 2015, his brother advised the Appellant that "other guys in Portugal had said they would deal with him (the Appellant)."2
When asked by the Delegate, "If there was work, would you go back to another area of Portugal?" the Appellant replied, "Yes, if there was work, I would go back." RPD's Reasons
In its reasons, the RPD found that the claim was not credible, that the Appellant's allegations were false and that the alleged threats were never made.

Pursuant to paragraph 111(1)(a) of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act (IRPA), the RAD confirms the decision of the RPD that the Appellant is neither a Convention refugee nor a person in need of protection. This appeal is dismissed. Appellant's Issues

Unfortunately, the Appellant has failed to put forward a comprehensive and informative memorandum, leaving the RAD in the position of trying to understand what the Appellant's issues are. This is not the job of the RAD. RAD Rule 3 clearly outlines what an Appellant must do in regards to an appeal record: (3) The appellant's record must contain the following documents, on consecutively numbered pages, in the following order: (a) the notice of decision and written reasons for the Refugee Protection Division's decision that the appellant is appealing; (b) all or part of the transcript of the Refugee Protection Division hearing if the appellant wants to rely on the transcript in the appeal, together with a declaration, signed by the transcriber, that includes the transcriber's name and a statement that the transcript is accurate; (c) any documents that the Refugee Protection Division refused to accept as evidence, during or after the hearing, if the appellant wants to rely on the documents in the appeal; (d) a written statement indicating (i) whether the appellant is relying on any evidence referred to in subsection 110(4) of the Act, (ii) whether the appellant is requesting that a hearing be held under subsection 110(6) of the Act, and if they are requesting a hearing, whether they are making an application under rule 66 to change the location of the hearing, and (iii) the language and dialect, if any, to be interpreted, if the Division decides that a hearing is necessary and the appellant needs an interpreter; (e) any documentary evidence that the appellant wants to rely on in the appeal; (f) any law, case law or other legal authority that the appellant wants to rely on in the appeal; and (g) a memorandum that includes full and detailed submissions regarding (i) the errors that are the grounds of the appeal, (ii) where the errors are located in the written reasons for the Refugee Protection Division's decision that the appellant is appealing or in the transcript or in any audio or other electronic recording of the Refugee Protection Division hearing, (iii) how any documentary evidence referred to in paragraph (e) meets the requirements of subsection 110(4) of the Act and how that evidence relates to the appellant, (iv) the decision the appellant wants the Division to make, and (v) why the Division should hold a hearing under subsection 110(6) of the Act if the appellant is requesting that a hearing be held.

The Appellant has supplied only a filled out copy of IRB/CISR 3005 form which gives only very basic and undetailed information on what the Appellant alleges are issues. This memorandum is deficient; however, I will do my best to work with this for the sake of fairness to the Appellant.

I believe the Appellant's issue is as follows: 1) Did the RPD err by failing to consider plausible explanations for the inconsistencies in the Appellant's behaviour and statements? ANALYSIS Determinative Issue

The determinative issue in this appeal is the Appellant's credibility. A second and equally determinative issue is state protection, which was canvassed at the hearing by the panel. Standard of Review
For questions of fact, mixed fact and law, and law, I have applied the standard of correctness as per Huruglica.3 Arguments
Counsel argues that the RPD erred when it did not consider what counsel argues is a plausible explanation for inconsistencies in the Appellant's behaviour and statements.

Counsel argues that it was a "combined effect" of the threats that the Appellant allegedly received in 2012 and the threat communicated over the phone in XXXX 2015 that triggered a credible and subjective fear in the Appellant.

However, I take note that one month after the XXXX 2015 phone threat, the Appellant still told the Minister's delegate that if there was work available in Portugal, the Appellant would return. This statement belies any allegation of being fearful for his life due to threats which the Appellant failed to tell CBSA about when he was interviewed by an agent. Counsel has argued that it was the combination of the 2012 threats and the 2015 threat that made the Appellant fearful enough to claim protection; however, the Appellant testified before the RPD that it was mainly because of the threats of 2012 that he came to Canada in March of 2012.

I also note that the Appellant did not even mention the 2012 threats in his Basis of Claim (BOC) form. The Appellant, when questioned by the panel on this failure to include a central issue of his claim in the BOC, testified that it was an issue with the translator who spoke very quickly and that the CBSA officer spoke quickly and did not want the Appellant to think. When the Appellant was asked how it was that he considered his BOC complete if he failed to include the threats which allegedly sent him fleeing to Canada, the Appellant testified that the CBSA officer did not ask those questions. However, the Appellant has testified that the CBSA officer was not present when the Appellant, with the help of his brother, completed his BOC.

Counsel argues that the omission of the critical fact of the 2012 threats from the BOC is understandable as "in the appellant's mind, the original threats in 2012 would have diminished over time and that it was his brother's XXXX 2015 communication that the threat still existed that triggered his fear." Counsel argues that it is therefore not unreasonable that the Appellant did not refer to the 2012 events in the Minister's Delegate review interview which took place in 2015.

I reject counsel's argument. It is not reasonable that the precipitating event which caused the Appellant to flee his home country, leaving his family behind, would not be mentioned in the interview and certainly not reasonable that such a catastrophic event which would send a man fleeing thousands of miles from his family and his home would not even rate a word in the BOC.

The Appellant has provided no evidence other than his testimony, to substantiate his claim. Counsel's argument is weak at best, nonsensical at worst. To suggest that the event which precipitated the Appellant's flight from Portugal would simply fade into the memory is ridiculous. Every day that the Appellant was in Canada, he was separated from loved-ones and from his homeland. To suggest that any person would forget about the reason he was so separated in a matter of a couple of years, while living away from loved ones, is implausible. I do not accept the explanation for the omission of critical information, central to the reason for his refugee claim, being omitted from his BOC.

Counsel has failed to indicate how or why the panel's decisions are either errors of fact or errors of law or errors of mixed fact and law. Counsel has simply argued an opinion (counsel's) of why he believes that the panel's decision is an error. That opinion is not substantiated by any evidence of error or by any case law. Counsel tells the RAD what counsel believes is an error but does not show the RAD how there is an error.

The RPD is allowed to make conclusions on credibility of witnesses, including claimants, based on such issues as omissions, inconsistencies, implausibilities and other reasons. Without evidence or at least case law to support counsel's arguments, the RAD will defer on issues of credibility where there is no contrary evidence presented and in the case where the RPD has a distinct advantage over the RAD in making the credibility determination. This is such a case.

The Appellant testified that he has no adequate state protection in Portugal, none would be forthcoming in Portugal and that he will not be able to avail himself of a viable internal flight alternative within Portugal. The Appellant failed to adduce any documentary evidence to support his allegation of inadequate state protection. This leaves the RAD in the position of depending solely upon the Division's National Documentary Package (NDP) for information on state protection.

I note that the 2017 OSAC Crime and Safety Report (U.S. D.O.S.),4 March 2017, states the following: Overall Crime and Safety Report "Portugal has a relatively low rate of violent crime..." Police Response "The authorities are professional..."

In another document,5 I find the following: Role of the Police and Security Apparatus The Ministries of Internal Administration and Justice are primarily responsible for internal security. The Ministry of Internal Administration oversees the SEF, the PSP, and the GNR. The SEF has jurisdiction over immigration and border problems. The PSP has jurisdiction in cities, and the GNR has jurisdiction outside cities. The PJ are responsible for criminal investigations and report to the Ministry of Justice. The IGAI, responsible to the Ministry of Internal Administration, investigates security force killings and evaluates whether they occurred in the line of duty or were otherwise justifiable. Civilian authorities maintained effective control over the SEF, the PSP, and the GNR, and the government has effective mechanisms to investigate and punish abuse and corruption. An independent ombudsman chosen by parliament and the IGAI investigates complaints of abuse or mistreatment by police. Nongovernmental organizations (NGOs) criticized the slow pace of investigations and the lack of an independent oversight agency to monitor the IGAI and the Ministry of Internal Administration.

In this same document, it is written as follows: Portugal, which includes the archipelagos of the Azores and Madeira, is a constitutional semi-presidential representative democracy with a president, prime minister, and parliament elected in multiparty elections. National legislative elections, held in October 2015, and presidential elections held on January 24 were free and fair. Civilian authorities maintained effective control over the security forces.

What all of the above tells me, and is unrefuted by any documentary evidence from the Appellant, is that Portugal is a democracy, fully functioning, and is able and willing to provide its citizens adequate state protection. That protection is and would be available to the Appellant should he need it. All there is for him to do is to ask. The Appellant has failed to adduce any evidence to support his allegation of inadequate state protection and has therefore failed to rebut the presumption. Presumption of state protection 1. States are presumed to be capable of protecting their citizens, except in situations where the state is in a state of complete breakdown. (Ward6) 2. The presumption that a state is capable of protecting its citizens underscores the principle that international protection comes into play only when a refugee claimant has no other recourse available. (Ward7) 3. The presumption of state protection applies equally to cases where the state is alleged to be a persecutor. (Hinzman8) Rebutting the presumption 4. To rebut the presumption of state protection, a claimant must provide "clear and convincing" evidence of the state's inability to protect its citizens, (absent an admission by the national's state of its inability to protect that national). (Ward9) 5. A claimant who alleges that the state protection is inadequate must persuade the Board that the evidence establishes that the state protection is inadequate. (Flores Carrillo10) The evidence that state protection is inadequate must not only be reliable and probative, it must also satisfy the Board, on a balance of probabilities, that the state protection is inadequate. (Flores Carrillo11) 6. Thus RPD is not obliged to prove that the state can offer the claimant effective protection, rather, the claimant bears the legal burden of rebutting the presumption that state protection exists by adducing clear and convincing evidence which satisfies the RPD on a balance of probabilities. (Kaleja12) 7. Where a state is in effective control of its territory, has military, police and civil authority in place and makes serious efforts to protect its citizens, the mere fact that the state's efforts are not always successful will not rebut the presumption of state protection. (Villafranca13) The Board is not obliged to prove that a state can offer its citizens effective state protection. (Quintero Sanchez14) Summary
The Appellant has failed to convince me that the RPD committed any errors of law, of fact or of mixed law and fact. I concur with the RPD that the Appellant lacks credibility and subjective fear.

Further, in the alternate, as state protection was canvassed during the hearing, it is reasonable for the RAD to consider that issue even if it was not expounded on in the Reasons and Decision, but only mentioned. The Appellant has not adduced any evidence before the RPD to support his allegation of inadequate state protection for him, in Portugal. I find that state protection in Portugal is at least adequate. Disposition
The RAD has found that the RPD decision will stand.

Pursuant to paragraph 111(1)(a) of the IRPA, the RAD confirms the decision of the RPD that the Appellant is neither a Convention refugee nor a person in need of protection. This appeal is dismissed.
